newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says it not helping Iran with missiles.
newsitem.headline: Russia says it not helping Iran with missiles.

text.p: Russia on Wednesday denied reports it was helping Iran develop ballistic missile technology.
"This is completely untrue," Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told a news conference following talks with Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz.
Aziz told reporters he was satisfied with Russia's policy when asked about reports that Moscow was helping to arm Baghdad's bitter rival.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that Israel planned to press Russia not to help Iran develop ballistic missiles.

"We view any assistance given by Russia to Iran to develop ballistic missiles as something that is inherently endangering the very future of Israel and we believe it also endangers the future and the interests of Russia," Netanyahu said.

The Los Angeles Times reported last month that U.S. intelligence reports indicated Russia recently transferred to Iran technology for the Russian SS-4 missile, which has a range almost three times greater than that of any missile now in Tehran's arsenal.
Asked for his reaction to a possible arming of Iran, Aziz responded: "The position of Russia is responsible."
The Iraqi minister was in Moscow to win support for the lifting of U.N. sanctions imposed on Baghdad after it invaded Kuwait in 1990. Primakov gave him the backing he was seeking.
"We hope that in this year all limitations...on the export of Iraqi oil will be lifted," Primakov said.
"In April a half-year stocktaking by the (U.N. arms monitoring) commission will take place, and we hope at this time, or just after this, any questions remaining will be removed," Primakov added.

Under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms, the ban on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted only if the U.N. Special Commission testifies that Baghdad has completely fulfilled all of its disarmament obligations.

As it anticipates a time when Iraq can freely sell its oil on international markets, Moscow plans to send a delegation of Energy Ministry officials to Iraq to discuss future oil ties and economic relations, Primakov said.
"We imagine that these negotiations will give a certain boost to our relations that will develop after the removal of the embargo," he said.
He also said that Russia supported a permanent extension of a oil-for-food deal that started last December allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil for humanitarian purposes.
Russia is expected to purchase about a quarter of this oil under contracts signed by seven Russian companies.
Aziz said that Iraq has met its disarmament obligations specified by the United Nations and blamed the United States and Great Britain for blocking the removal of the embargo.
"We have fulfilled all the obligations imposed by the international community," he said. "Iraq does not threaten anyone."

Primakov, a Middle East expert who became foreign minister in January 1996, has sought to improve Russian ties with allies of the former Soviet Union such as Iraq in what he calls a "diversification" of Moscow's foreign policy.
